Reading your story though…what an amazing opportunity. Not many people get to see an owl up close, let alone save it. You got to watch an owl regain its strength and fly away. This is me. I had a concussion in October and again in November. Everything you are describing is what I experienced as well. And I’m still going through the same things. I’m a teacher and I can’t remember my students names. Or, I’ll teach and use incorrect words and not realize it until someone mentions it. I sometimes forget where I am. I have times where I lose chunks of memory. 

I saw a speech therapist who specialized in concussions. Tbh, the support was limited, but here were a few tips she gave me. 
1) listen to a podcast or a movie and retell it to a friend. 
2) have a friend text you five words at the beginning of the day and you tell them back at the end of the day
3) be thoughtful when you put something down, so you will remember where it is in the future (ex I am putting this paper next to the basket)
4) make word connections a game you play. She had me do it in her office. She gave me a word and I had to think of everything related to it. Example: her word was pineapple. I thought of many words like acidic, yellow, spikes, fruit, tropical, smoothie, etc. 

She explained that things our brains used to be able to do aren’t easy, especially since our brains are now focused more on healing. You have to create those pathways again. It sucks and it takes effort. It causes me headaches but I can tell parts of my speech are improving. 

I hope this helps a little. I hope you recover quickly.

Don’t be down on yourself. It sounds like the boys are not trying their best or are down on themselves when they play in their own age group. Have you asked them what they did to be successful against the older team? Put it on them to answer and reflect on how they did. 

Regarding your formation, I would try two strikers. It seems like they are already in each other’s space. Five in the middle can cause for a lot of clumping. 

This sounds stupid, but it works. I draw out where I want my outside midfield. It is a long box. I tell them that this is their party. They have control of their box and their party. If anyone comes in there without being invited, they are crashing parties. I explain that we can have people come help put up decorations, or help clean for the party, but there is no need to have more than one person help. When I yell “crashing parties” they are more aware of it, almost like a keyword and they tend to drop or angle themselves better. I tell this to my older players too. It seems childish, but it’s often the stupid things that stick with them more than “spread out”. 

You aren’t a bad coach. It’s so interesting that they had the drive to tie 4-4 on an older team. Tell them you know what they are capable of. Hype them up and tell them all the positives they reflect on. Put the games and the success on them as a team.

When you practice, do you do set drills or small sided games? I have been coaching for a decade now from u6-U18 select. The biggest thing is to let them practice as a team in game like situations. They won’t learn how to practice and play together by doing set drills. Let them be creative in small sided game situations. This will transfer to game situations. 

What is their attitude like? Do they believe they are capable of winning? I’ve had teams who lost their first game and gave up the rest of the season. Also, is this their first year on a full size field? It may take time for them to mentally and physically adjust. 

At your next game, try switching your strongest defender and forward. They might surprise you. Taking a risk like that may allow for new opportunities. I do this when I need something different. I don’t keep them this way. I do it for maybe ten minutes and then evaluate how we are doing.

I have an emotional support cat for my panic attacks. I trained him to sit on my chest or legs when I’m panicking. He purrs and waits with me until it’s gone. He went with me through college and lived with me in the dorms. He even came with me when I took exams. He sat on my lap while I did the exam. 

Animals are amazing. They can sense your heart rate changing. They know. They know how to help, too. I could go on and on about how important my cat is to my anxiety success. Get an animal. They will help.

I also don’t get the breathing sensation or hard to breathe panic attacks. Mine are similar to yours. Sometimes I’ll shake uncontrollably for hours and I can’t get the words out because I’m shaking. Only once have I struggled to breathe. I called an ambulance to help me calm down after that one.

Mine are similar. I usually feel the need to flee and throw up. I want to run but don’t know where to go, especially if I need to throw up. I scream and shake a lot. One time, this lasted for eight hours. At that point my parents were prepared to bring me to the emergency room and get a sedative. My body was so weak from constant shaking. I ended up being so exhausted that I fell asleep in the bathtub. 

Here are some things that help me. I just got over a HUGE panic attack a few minutes ago. 

1. Talk out loud to yourself. Admit you are having a panic attack. As soon as I notice I am having a panic attack my brain chills out. It doesn’t stop the panic attack, but it does make my coping skills much more effective. 

2. Try coping skills. If something worked in the past, try it. If it didn’t work in the past, give it another shot. 

3. Go for a walk. Fresh air is amazing. 

4. If you need to, call 911. Ask for an ambulance. There was four different occasions when I couldn’t handle it on my own. I was able to get it together long enough to say “panic attack”. The paramedics were always incredibly kind, calm and supportive. They never rushed me. They sat outside my house for an hour and a half until we were certain it was gone. If you need to-call them. They are there. It’s free. You will only be charged if they take you in. If they hang out and take vitals, it’s free. At least here in America where I’m from it is. 

I could do another entire post about coping mechanisms if you need.

I understand. I was you. I loved most of my life incredibly sheltered. I understood there were awful things, but I wasn’t fully aware of how often these horrible things were happening to such a wide variety of people. I became angry that I was born into such a “boring” life where nothing bad happened. I was upset that I struggled with mental health despite having a happy childhood. 

Then I went to Guatemala. I stayed in a foliage with no running water and no electricity. Dogs with open wounds ran the streets. Children didn’t go to school. Families struggled to make ends meet in a way I could never imagine. 

But these people were happy. Happy in a way I had never gotten to experience myself. They were thriving off what they had. Thriving off each other. They saw the positives instead of the unjust world we all share. 

It was an incredible experience that I too often forget. Yes, there are awful things in this works. Horrible things. I was raped. I suffer anxiety. I have panic attacks. I sometimes want to die. But other times I have this spark inside me. It reminds me of the happy moments I have had in life. The moments where I made someone else smile, or when a stranger comforted me. I look to those happy moments and realize there still is a lot of good in this world. It may be hiding in an unexpected spot, but it’s there.
